blocks.text: REST is the underlying HTTP-based architectural style most LLM APIs are built on, structured URLs, standard HTTP methods, headers carrying authentication, and a JSON request and response body, this topic covers these mechanics directly, building on the API architecture concepts covered in an earlier topic.

This topic covers the HTTP methods LLM APIs actually use, URL and endpoint structure, headers for authentication and content type, the JSON request body, and what HTTP status codes signal about a request outcome.
1. What REST Means for an LLM API

blocks.alt: Building on SDKs, REST APIs cover the underlying HTTP foundation

blocks.text: REST, representational state transfer, is an architectural style built on standard HTTP, using URLs to identify resources or actions and standard HTTP methods to interact with them, most LLM APIs, and the SDKs covered in the previous topic that wrap them, are built on this same REST foundation underneath.
2. HTTP Methods, Mostly POST

blocks.alt: GET retrieves data, POST sends data and generates a response

blocks.text: While REST supports several HTTP methods, LLM API calls that actually generate a response typically use POST, since generating a completion involves sending substantial data, the prompt and settings, GET requests are more commonly used for simpler operations like listing available models.

code.content:
# POST to generate a response
POST https://api.example.com/v1/chat/completions

# GET to list available models
GET https://api.example.com/v1/models

blocks.text: 3. URL Structure and Endpoints

blocks.alt: A base URL combines with an endpoint path to form the full request URL

blocks.text: This connects directly to the endpoints concept covered in the earlier API Architecture topic, a full request URL combines a base URL, identifying the provider service, with a specific endpoint path identifying which capability you are actually calling, chat completions, embeddings, or models.
4. Headers, Authentication and Content Type

blocks.alt: An Authorization header and a Content-Type header both matter for a REST request

blocks.text: This connects directly to authentication and API keys, both covered elsewhere in this module, the Authorization header typically carries the API key proving the request is legitimate, the Content-Type header tells the server the request body is JSON, both are required for nearly every LLM API call.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Header","Purpose"],"rows":[["Authorization","Proves the request is legitimate, typically carrying an API key"],["Content-Type","Tells the server the request body format, usually JSON"]]}

blocks.text: 5. The JSON Request Body

blocks.alt: A JSON request body contains the prompt and settings

blocks.text: This connects directly to JSON generation, covered in an earlier module, the actual prompt, conversation history, and configuration settings, model choice, temperature, maximum tokens, all get sent as a JSON object in the request body, this is the structured payload the model actually processes.
6. HTTP Status Codes and What They Signal

blocks.alt: 200 signals success, 400 a bad request, 429 rate limited, 500 a server error

blocks.text: This connects directly to rate limiting, covered elsewhere in this module, the HTTP status code returned with every response tells your application what actually happened, 200 for success, 400 for a malformed request, 429 specifically signaling a rate limit was hit, 500 for a provider side server error, handling each of these appropriately is standard, necessary practice.

blocks.title: Status codes deserve explicit handling, not just checking for success
blocks.content: An application that only checks for a 200 success status and treats everything else identically misses genuinely useful information, a 429 rate limit response usually warrants a retry after a delay, a 400 bad request usually indicates a bug in the request itself worth fixing, not retrying blindly.

blocks.text: 7. REST vs the Streaming Alternative

blocks.alt: REST is typically synchronous by default, the streaming alternative is covered next

blocks.text: A standard REST call, as covered in this topic, typically waits for the complete response before returning, streaming APIs, covered in the next topic, extend this same underlying REST foundation with a different response delivery pattern, returning content incrementally rather than all at once.
8. A Worked REST Request Example

A complete request to generate a response combines a POST method, the correct endpoint URL, an Authorization header carrying the API key, a Content-Type header specifying JSON, and a JSON body containing the model name and conversation messages, every one of these pieces has to be correct for the request to succeed.
9. REST as the Common Foundation Across Providers

This connects directly to the provider specific modules covered later in this course, while each provider, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, uses its own specific endpoint paths and JSON field names, they all share this same underlying REST foundation, understanding these mechanics here makes each provider specific module far easier to follow.
Worked Example

A developer new to working with LLM APIs initially struggles to understand why a request fails, after checking the actual raw HTTP details, they discover their request was missing the Content-Type header, causing the server to misinterpret the JSON body entirely.

Understanding the full REST request structure, method, URL, headers, and body, each playing a distinct required role, lets them diagnose this exact class of issue quickly going forward, rather than guessing blindly at what might be wrong.
Common Mistakes

items: Omitting a required header, like Content-Type or Authorization, and getting a confusing error as a result
Treating every non-200 status code identically instead of handling each one, like 429 rate limits, appropriately
Using the wrong HTTP method for a given endpoint, GET where POST is expected or vice versa
Not understanding the underlying REST structure well enough to debug an issue when an SDK abstraction encounters a problem

blocks.text: Practice

Take an SDK call you have made or seen before, and sketch out the equivalent raw REST request it likely makes underneath, the HTTP method, the URL, the required headers, and the JSON body shape, to build a clearer mental model of what the SDK is actually doing for you.
Key Takeaway

REST APIs use standard HTTP methods, structured URLs, headers for authentication and content type, and a JSON body carrying the actual prompt and settings, this shared foundation underlies nearly every LLM provider API, and understanding it directly makes both raw API calls and SDK abstractions, both covered in this module, much easier to work with and debug.
